text: The Ainu are the Indigenous people of northern Japan and nearby parts of Russia.
They call their homeland Ainu Mosir, and their name means “human being”.
src: The Ainu are the Indigenous people of Hokkaido, Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands / The Ainu are an Indigenous people of northern Japan and southeastern Russia
who call their homeland Ainu Mosir, “the land of the Ainu” / Their name, Aynu, means “human being” or “person”

text: Their culture took shape about 800 years ago, from older cultures of the north.
src: whose own culture took shape around the 13th century / Historians generally link the rise of Ainu culture to the Satsumon culture ... with later contributions from the Okhotsk culture of the north

text: They lived in small villages called kotan, beside rivers where salmon swam upstream.
They fished for salmon, hunted deer and bears, and grew millet.
src: Ainu society was built around small villages called kotan, usually of fewer than ten households, set along rivers where salmon ran upstream
They hunted Ezo deer, Ussuri brown bears and Asian black bears / Salmon was called kamuy chep, “god’s fish” / They also grew millets

text: For the Ainu, everything in nature holds a kamuy, a spirit or god.
Lacquer bowls from Honshu were treasured and used to offer drink to the kamuy.
src: The Ainu are traditionally animists: everything in nature holds a kamuy, a spirit or god
Lacquerware, almost all imported from Honshu, was treasured and used for offering drink to the kamuy

text: They wove robes from tree bark, and women wore necklaces of glass beads.
src: The attus robe was woven from bark fibre / Women wore embroidered headbands (matanpushi), earrings and necklaces of glass beads called tamasay, some from the Asian mainland

text: Later, Japanese rulers took much of their land and banned their language and religion.
Today Japan’s law recognises them as an Indigenous people, and craftswomen still weave traditional clothes.
src: Japanese colonisation brought land seizure, forced labour, family separation, epidemics and bans on language and religion
Japan passed recognition into law in 2019 / Modern craftswomen still weave and embroider traditional garments
